To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sex difference in sensitivity to nicotine in mice is not related to differences in blood or brain levels of nicotine, but may be related to differences in the distribution or metabolism of the drug.
the sexes differ significantly in their sensitivity to convulsant doses of nicotine and that the age of the animals also influences their sensitivity to the convulsant effects of nicotine.

the sexes differ markedly in their behavioral responses to nicotine, that the sexes differ only slightly in brain levels of nicotine and that blood levels of the drug do not correlate with either the brain levels or the behavioral responses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the behavioral response to nicotine and the blood and brain levels in mice.
the relationship of blood and brain levels to behavioral responses to nicotine and the influence of sex and strain on this relationship.
the pharmacokinetics of nicotine in two inbred mouse strains and the behavioral responses to this drug.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the blood level of nicotine does not accurately reflect brain levels of nicotine nor the behavioral responses to this drug in mice.
the sex differences in sensitivity to nicotine are not related to differences in brain levels of nicotine.
sex and age differences exist in the sensitivity of mice to nicotine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

sex and age differences exist in the behavioral and pharmacokinetic responses to nicotine in mice, but the behavioral responses do not correlate with the blood or brain levels of nicotine in the mice.
the behavioral response to a single dose of nicotine is related to brain levels of nicotine, but not blood levels, and that the sex differences are related to brain concentration of nicotine.
sex differences in the behavioral responses to acute doses of nicotine are not related to sex differences in blood and brain levels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sex differences in the brain levels of nicotine do not necessarily translate into differences in sensitivity to the drug.
the blood level of nicotine is not a reliable predictor of the behavioral response to a single dose of nicotine.
the sex of the animal must be considered when studying the behavioral and neuropharmacological effects of nicotine.
